title: Electronic Symmetry and Femtosecond Coherence Dynamics of Renner-Teller-Mixed Neutral Vibronic States in Carbon Dioxide
authors: Eric Liu, Shashank Kumar, Siddhant Pandey, Tzu-Hsien Tan, Russell Zimmerman, Kousik Bera, Anthony Fiore, Paul Hockett, Varun Makhija, Niranjan Shivaram
abstract: When non-adiabatic coupling mixes electronic states of a molecule, vibronic states of different electronic symmetry become interleaved across the same spectral region. The symmetry of these states cannot be accessed in conventional spectroscopy due to orientation averaging. We show that molecular-frame angular signatures, which are preserved even when states with different symmetry overlap in energy, can be used to resolve them. Using vacuum-ultraviolet transient absorption spectroscopy of aligned carbon dioxide molecules, we separate two electronically distinct classes of vibronic states ($A^{'}$ and $A^{''}$) that arise from Renner-Teller splitting of the $^1Δ_u$ state. We reconstruct molecular-frame anisotropy continuously across the vibronic manifold showing that the anisotropy crosses over from perpendicular to parallel transition character and maps the interleaved electronic symmetry landscape. By scanning the femtosecond delay between the VUV and a near-infrared pulse through temporal overlap, we measure symmetry-dependent coherence dephasing times of these states and find that the parallel ($A^{'}$) states dephase faster than the perpendicular ($A^{''}$) states. We attribute this to faster departure of the $A^{'}$ wavepacket from the Franck-Condon region due to the distinct topology of the $A^{'}$ excited-state surface. These measurements probe symmetry-resolved ultrafast wavepacket dynamics on the coupled excited-state potential energy surfaces.
summary: The researchers used VUV transient absorption on aligned $	ext{CO}_2$ to study vibronic states split by the Renner-Teller effect. By analyzing molecular-frame angular signatures, they separated states based on their electronic symmetry ($A'$ vs. $A''$). They found that the coherence lifetime differs between these symmetry classes, providing direct evidence that the excited-state potential energy surface topology dictates the rate of wavepacket dephasing.
main_problem: To resolve and characterize the symmetry-dependent ultrafast dynamics of vibronic states in molecules where electronic states are mixed due to non-adiabatic coupling.
main_result: The parallel ($A'$) vibronic states dephase measurably faster than the perpendicular ($A''$) states, which is attributed to the distinct, anharmonic topology of the $A'$ excited-state potential energy surface.
method: Vacuum-ultraviolet (VUV) transient absorption spectroscopy of aligned $	ext{CO}_2$ molecules, combined with molecular-frame angular signature analysis.
model_or_system: The system is $	ext{CO}_2$ undergoing Renner-Teller splitting, leading to vibronic states ($A'$ and $A''$). Dynamics are probed by measuring coherence dephasing times ($	au_d$) across the vibronic manifold.
key_observables: Molecular-frame anisotropy ($c_2/c_0$), differential absorption spectrum ($\Delta	ext{OD}$), and symmetry-dependent coherence dephasing times ($	au_d$).
important_parameters: Femtosecond delay ($	au$) between VUV and NIR pulses; the energy difference between $A'$ and $A''$ states.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on reconstructing molecular-frame information from lab-frame measurements and modeling the coherence decay using an Exponentially Modified Gaussian (EMG) distribution.
figures_summary: Figures show $\Delta	ext{OD}$ vs. delay $	au$ revealing rotational dynamics, anisotropy plots confirming parallel/perpendicular character, and $	au_d$ vs. energy plots demonstrating the symmetry-dependent decay rates.
paper_structure: The paper systematically uses alignment-resolved VUV transient absorption to first map the symmetry landscape via anisotropy, and then uses time-resolved measurements to extract symmetry-specific coherence dephasing times, linking these lifetimes to the underlying potential energy surface topology.
why_interesting: This work provides a direct, ultrafast spectroscopic method to map out the symmetry-resolved dynamics on coupled excited-state potential energy surfaces, which is crucial for understanding non-adiabatic processes in molecular physics.
